1:
Four voices notice the same irony. Theophylact states it first: the Pharisees tried to catch Jesus in his talk "that they might lead away the people from Him. But this design of theirs is reversed" — "so mighty a thing is truth, so feeble every where deceit". Henry says the same: "the more the Pharisees strove to drive the people from Christ, the more flocking there was to him." Barnes generalises: Jesus "never had more to hear him than when he was most faithful and severe in his reproofs of sinners", since "men's consciences are on the side of the faithful reprover". Robertson agrees the crowd was "drawn together by the violent attacks of the rabbis".

How large a crowd nobody will say. Clarke does the arithmetic and abandons it — a myriad is ten thousand, so the plural means twenty thousand at least, "but the word is often used to signify a crowd... which cannot be readily numbered". Lightfoot is blunter: "there is no one would understand this in the very letter of it."

What "first of all" governs divides them. Barnes insists it is priority, not audience — it means "above all things beware", not before all others. Wesley reads it of the audience, disciples first and the people afterwards, and Robertson agrees, taking the talk to run through verse twelve.

Why leaven is the figure gets the same answer twice. Barnes lists its properties — undetected, insinuating, swelling, so "no man is more proud than the hypocrite" — and Henry has it "swelling and souring as leaven, for it puffs men up with pride, embitters them with malice". Clarke reports a doubt the others do not raise, that "which is hypocrisy" may be an addition, since Christ may have objected to Pharisaic doctrine rather than pretence; his verdict is that "they had, however, a large proportion of both".

Ellicott then makes the finest distinction here. Hypocrisy means unreality, "the simulation, conscious or unconscious, of a holiness which we do not possess" — and it does not follow "that the Pharisees were deliberate impostors of the Tartuffe type", since with them "the worst hypocrisy was that which did not know itself to be hypocritical". Robertson keeps to history: it was the leading Pharisaic vice, "a mark of sanctity to hide an evil heart".

Henry asks why the disciples needed the warning, and answers three ways: they professed more than others; they were to preach, and a deceitful preacher corrupts the word; and "there was a Judas among them, who was a hypocrite, and Christ knew it, and would hereby startle him, or leave him inexcusable". Its being said publicly he takes as deliberate, "to let the world know that he would not countenance hypocrisy, no, not in his own disciples".

On the next clause Ellicott corrects the English: the Greek conjunction "cannot possibly have the meaning of for", so the sense is not a reason but a warning laid alongside — "beware ye of hypocrisy; but, whether ye beware or not, know that all that is now secret will one day be manifested". He renders it "there is nothing veiled that shall not be unveiled", and notes that the same saying carries opposite force in Matthew, where the coming disclosure encourages open preaching while here it discourages counterfeits — the third verse turning the same way, the disciples being hearers bound to publish there, teachers accountable for every whisper here.

Robertson, facing the same duplication, puts the alternative bluntly: either Jesus repeated himself often, or "the Gospels have hopelessly jumbled" these sayings "as to time and place". Lightfoot draws the moral: "in time the visor shall be taken off." Gill agrees no sin is more covered than hypocrisy, nor more surely detected. Tertullian, against Marcion, takes the Son to be defending his Father's honour, since it was the Creator the Pharisees sinned against.
4:
Ambrose explains why the warning stands here. Unbelief "springs from two causes, either from a deeply-seated malice or a sudden fear", and having met the malice Christ now guards the other, "lest any one from terror should be compelled to deny the God whom he acknowledges in his heart". He adds the calculation that makes martyrdom rational: "that death is not terrible for which at a far more costly rate of interest immortality is to be purchased."

Cyril of Alexandria limits the audience: the discourse applies not "absolutely to every one, but to those who love God with their whole heart", the rest "tottering, and ready to fall down". Robertson notes that friends is set against the Pharisees just rebuked.

That the command to fear God is addressed to friends strikes Clarke and Wesley the same way. Clarke: "even the friends of God are commanded to fear God", and a man "has but one life to lose, and one soul to save; and it is madness to sacrifice the salvation of the soul to the preservation of the life". Wesley concludes that this fear "is to be pressed even on true believers".

Calvin insists the two clauses be read together, since only the contrast carries the argument: "when we give way to the dread of men, we pay no respect to God", and if we fear God "we have an easy victory in our hands". God allows the wicked "such a degree of liberty, that they are swelled with confidence in their own power", but their supposing "the life of the godly were placed at their disposal, is utterly unfounded". Nor is the fear theoretical: "Satan brings forward giants, in whose presence the servants of Christ would fall down lifeless, were it not that this doctrine fortifies them."

Theophylact reads the clause in a direction none of the others would follow. Christ "says not, 'Who casts into hell,' but has power to cast" — whence "not every one dying in sin is forthwith thrust down into hell, but there is sometimes pardon given for the sake of the offerings and prayers which are made for the dead". Robertson stays with the place-name: Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom, where children were passed through the fire to Molech until Josiah abolished it and it became a rubbish tip burning ceaselessly, "a symbol of punishment in the other world".

The sparrows produce arithmetic. Clarke works the proportion — one farthing buys two, two farthings five — and Gill supplies the reason, that "where more money is laid out, things are bought cheaper". Ellicott hears the haggling: the sparrow "was of so little value that the odd bird was thrown in to tempt the purchasers". He turns the discrepancy into an argument, since this and the difference between falling to the ground in Matthew and being forgotten before God here are "proofs, again, of the independence of the two Gospels".

Lightfoot asks why sparrows were on sale at all. Doves were sold at the Temple for women after childbirth, so he supposes sparrows were sold for cleansing lepers, reporting without endorsement R. Solomon's "far-fetched reason" that leprosy came of an evil tongue, so that the cleansing used birds "that are always chirping and chattering with their voice". His second note is the finest: R. Simeon Ben Jochai, at his cave mouth, watched a fowler — when the voice from heaven said "Mercy", the bird escaped; when it said "The pain of death", the bird was taken.

Origen allegorises the five as the spiritual senses, "lightly esteemed by those who count as perishing whatever is of the Spirit"; Theophylact offers a rival key, the two Testaments. Gill keeps the plain sense, the numbered hairs meaning not one can fall "without the knowledge and will of God"; Clarke names the root of the anxiety, that man distrusts God "because he judges of God by himself".
8:
Bede supplies the join: the previous verses said every hidden work would be revealed, this says where — "in the presence of the heavenly city and the eternal Judge and King". Ambrose notices faith comes in with its support attached — "as faith is the incentive to fortitude, so is fortitude the strong support of faith" — and Chrysostom that inward belief is not accepted alone: "the Lord is not then content with an inward faith, but requires an outward confession."

What must be confessed Cyril of Alexandria states from Paul and calls the whole mystery of Christ: that the Word born of the Father is Lord "not as one who had gained His Lordship from without and by stealth, but who is in truth by His nature Lord", and that God raised him who "was Himself truly made man, and suffered in the flesh for us". The deniers he sorts in two: those who renounce under persecution, and "heretical teachers also, and their disciples".

Chrysostom widens that class: denial includes professing to know God while denying him in works, failing to provide for one's own house, and covetousness — "since then there are so many modes of denial, it is plain that there are many likewise of confession." He then finds in a preposition an asymmetry none of the moderns notice: the Greek has confess in me, "showing that not by his own strength, but by the aid of grace from above, a man confesses Christ", but of the denier "He said not 'in Me,' but me", a man denying out of his own destitution.

Gill guards the point pastorally: a man may deny Christ and afterwards confess him, and "through temptation, a real Christian may be left for a while... to deny him and his truths, and afterwards truly repent, and at last be saved, as Peter". What is fatal is denying publicly and persisting.

Lightfoot separates two sins commonly run together. Both are unpardonable, but "apostasy cannot properly be charged on any but who have already professed Christianity", whereas the blasphemy "was uttered by the scribes and Pharisees at that time that they disowned and rejected Christ" — one a defection from within, the other an attack from outside. Wesley states the gradation simply: denial "in some degree, may, upon true repentance, be forgiven", blasphemy against the Spirit never — "neither is there place for repentance".

Whether these words belong here is contested three ways. Gill says they were spoken when the Pharisees ascribed Christ's works to Beelzebub, and are only recorded here by Luke. Ellicott agrees they were first uttered then, but thinks them "repeated in their more general bearing" here. Robertson refuses the assumption behind the question: Luke "apparently finds a different environment here", and "there is no sound reason for saying that Jesus only spoke his memorable sayings once".

On the promise of what to say under trial, Ellicott notices the scope has grown — "what had been a special promise to the Twelve is now extended to all whom the Lord calls His friends" — and adds a philological point: the pairing of authorities and powers recurs in Luke and four Pauline letters, one of the phrases which "had passed from the Evangelist to the Apostle, or conversely". Robertson blocks the abuse: it "is no excuse for neglect in pulpit preparation. It is simply a word for courage in a crisis."

Cyril of Jerusalem makes the passage evidence for the Spirit's own work. If no man can call Jesus Lord but by the Holy Ghost, then "it is impossible to testify as a martyr for Christ's sake, except a man testify by the Holy Ghost" — "how shall any man give his own life for Jesus' sake, but by the Holy Ghost?" The confession is itself the Spirit's — hence the gravity of the sin against him.
13:
Ambrose explains the join: the previous verses armed the disciples for suffering, and "since covetousness is generally wont to try virtue, for destroying this also, a precept and example is added." Theophylact supplies the situation uncharitably — two brothers contending over a patrimony, so "it follows that one meant to defraud the other" — and Gill notes that some versions soften the address to friend.

The vocative is where two commentators eleven centuries apart converge. Bede takes man as rebuke: one who would impose the trouble of dividing lands "upon the Master who is commending the joys of heavenly peace, is rightly called man", by the apostle's rule that where there is strife "are you not men?" Ellicott, independently, calls this "the only instance of our Lord's so addressing one who had come to Him as a questioner", the form expressing "grave censure and indignation" — was this what men came to him for "instead of seeking for the kingdom of God"?

Ambrose presses this into a rule for petitioners: "you should consider then, not what you seek, but from whom you ask it." The request is wrong twice over: between brothers "no judge should intervene, but natural affection should be the umpire", and the patrimony worth waiting for is immortality, not riches. Cyril of Alexandria puts it as commission: the Son was appointed "to be King and Prince upon his holy Mount of Sion", not to arbitrate estates.

Calvin alone gives a political reason, and it is the sharpest offered. The Jews expected an earthly Messiah; had Christ been seen dividing an inheritance, "many would have been led to expect a carnal redemption... and wicked men would have loudly declared, that he was effecting a revolution in the state, and overturning the Roman Empire". The reply forestalled both, informing all "that the kingdom of Christ is spiritual", and yields a maxim: undertake nothing "which may admit of an unfavorable construction".

Barnes and Clarke both turn the refusal into a rule for the ministry, by different routes. Barnes argues from jurisdiction: Jesus could have said what was right, "but then it would have been interfering with the proper office of the magistrates", so ministers should "attend to spiritual concerns". Clarke argues from consequence, and more shrewdly: "he who preaches salvation to all should never make himself a party man; otherwise he loses the confidence, and consequently the opportunity of doing good to the party against whom he decides" — allowing one exception, where a lawsuit may be prevented and both sides satisfied.

On the warning Clarke has a textual case. He would read all covetousness, adding the word on the authority of the older uncials, twenty-three copies and most of the versions — and glosses the Greek as more plus to have, so the vice is "the desire to have more and more, let a person possess whatever he may", a disposition "never satisfied; for, as soon as one object is gained, the heart goes out after another". Bede reached the same word from another side: "some things seem to be honestly done, but the internal judge decides with what intention they are done."

What "life" means in the closing sentence is a real disagreement. Barnes states the alternative and rejects it: some take life as happiness, "but this meaning does not suit the parable following, which is designed to show that property will not lengthen out a man's life", so the word "is to be taken literally". Wesley reads it exactly as Barnes forbids — "that is, the comfort or happiness of it". Calvin goes behind the word to the belief that feeds the vice, that "a man is happy in proportion as he possesses much", whence "arise those immoderate desires, which, like a fiery furnace, send forth their flames". Clarke settles for the practical: "it is not superfluities that support man's life, but necessaries."
16:
Theophylact states the parable's office plainly: having said that life is not extended by abundance, Christ "adds a parable to induce belief in this". Ellicott notices its texture rather than its function — like the Good Samaritan it is "more than a similitude, and reads like an actual history", with "an almost dramatic vividness in the rich man's soliloquy".

Basil begins with the crop itself. The ground yielded plentifully not because the man deserved it but so "that the mercy of God might the more appear, which extends its goodness even to the bad; sending down His rain upon the just and the unjust" — after which the question is what he repaid. Nothing: "he remembered not his fellow-creatures, nor deemed that he ought to give of his superfluities to the needy", and though the barns were bursting "yet was his greedy mind by no means satisfied".

The sharpest thing Basil says concerns the wording of the complaint. "His complaint is like that of the poor. Does not the man oppressed with want say, What shall I do, whence can I get food, whence clothing? Such things also the rich man utters." The distress is real but inverted: he is anxious "lest perchance when they have come forth they should profit the poor" — "like the glutton who had rather burst from eating, than give any thing of what remains to the starving".

Gregory compresses it into four words — "O adversity, the child of plenty" — then turns the man's plan against him. Pulling the barns down is a good idea: "the storehouses of iniquity are worthy of destruction. Pull down your barns, from which no one receives comfort." The rebuilding is folly, since "if you shall complete these, will you again destroy them? What more foolish than laboring on for ever." His alternative is one sentence — "your barns, if you will, are the home of the poor" — and he meets the property argument, "whom do I wrong by keeping what is my own?", with a counter-question: "tell me what is yours, from whence did you get it?"

That wealth brings anxiety rather than relieving it is agreed across every school here. Ellicott puts it as arithmetic: "it was the very superfluity of the man's goods that became a new cause of anxiety. In such a case half was more than the whole." Barnes says riches "increase thought and perplexity", and "indeed, this is almost their only effect — to engross the thoughts and steal the heart away from better things"; Clarke, that riches "though ever so well acquired, produce nothing but vexation and embarrassment", and that the rich "take no thought about eternity till the time that their goods and their lives are both taken away".

Robertson counts the pronouns and finds the indictment in them: "my fruits, my barns, my corn, my goods, just like Nabal whose very name means fool." Gill reads the soliloquy the same way — the man "consults himself only", never asking what God would have him do with the increase, and "nor did he think even of his own soul, but altogether about his worldly substance".

The lesser notes are philological. Barnes explains that the Greek covers all produce and not fruit only, "this is likewise the old meaning of the English word"; Ellicott that the barns are storehouses of any kind, the Greek being the word "whence our apothecary"; Robertson that the corn is grain, "not maize or Indian corn", and the goods simply good things, as in a goods train. Barnes also answers the question the story invites — why not build beside the old barns? — by noting that ancient granaries were dug underground, safer from thieves and vermin, so enlarging an excavation was easier than sinking a new one.
19:
Gill notices who is addressed: the man speaks to his soul but means "his sensual appetite, which he sought to indulge and gratify, for he was wholly a sensual and carnal man" — the highest thing in him addressed as though it were the lowest.

Barnes and Clarke identify the creed in almost the same words. Barnes calls it "just the doctrine of the ancient Epicureans and atheists", too often that of the rich; Clarke, "exactly the creed of the ancient Atheists and Epicureans", quoting their tag that after death there is no pleasure. Both break off into the same exclamation — Barnes's "what a portion is this for an immortal soul!" against Clarke's "what a wretched portion for an immortal spirit!" — and Clarke adds that those who know not God "have no other, and many of them not even this". Barnes turns his into a picture of modern appetite — the delicacies of the season, "the productions of every clime at any expense" — for a creature with "an intellect to be cultivated, a heart to be purified, a soul to be saved". Ellicott notes that Paul quoted the same words. Clarke adds a judgement few would print: "moderate poverty, as one justly observes, is a great talent in order to salvation; but it is one which nobody desires."

Lightfoot brings a rabbinic ruling that catches the man exactly. When the church is in distress, none may say "I will go into mine house, and will eat and drink, and peace be to thee, O my soul", for of such it is written that he joined those who said "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die", and heard the answer, "surely this iniquity shall not be purged away from you till you die". Then Lightfoot asks the worse question: "and what if he should so say and do when the church is not in distress?"

How the sentence reached him Gill leaves open, offering three mechanisms: God "determined within himself he should die that night", or "sent the messenger of death, some disease or another", or "spoke to his conscience". What is not open is the timing, "for the time of a man's death, as well as of his birth, is fixed by God".

His second story he introduces with an apology — it "hath something in it that may be laughed at, yet hath it something in it that is serious enough". Rabbi Simeon Ben Chalaphta feasted at a circumcision where the father poured wine seven years old and said, "with this wine will I grow old in the joy of my son." At midnight the rabbi met the angel of death and found him sad. Why? "I am sad for the speeches of those who say, I will do this or that ere long, though they know not how quickly they may be called away by death."

Barnes reads the verdict as exposed arithmetic: "if there is any supreme folly, it is this. As though riches could prolong life" — and the goods, which cannot buy "one moment's ease", pass to heirs who "dissipate them much sooner than the father procured them".

On the application Gill and Barnes describe the same man from two sides. Gill: he "employs all his thoughts, and spends all his time, in amassing to himself worldly riches", and "makes no use of his earthly substance to be the good of others". Barnes's sharpest inference is that the covetous man's anxiety "is not what good he may do with his wealth, but where he may hoard it, and keep it secure from doing any good" — a fear of the money proving useful. His conclusion inverts the parable's terror: if the affections are not fixed on riches "we shall leave them without regret", and if the treasure is in heaven, death "will be but going home".
22:
Theophylact reads the chapter as a graded advance: "the Lord carries us onward by degrees to a more perfect teaching." First came the warning against covetousness, then the parable showing "that the fool is he who desires more than is enough", and now the prohibition reaches even necessary things, "plucking out the very root of covetousness".

He is careful about the odd phrase that follows. The soul is told not to be anxious what it shall eat — "not that the intellectual soul eats, but because there seems no other way for the soul to dwell united to the body except by being nourished". Why the body gets its own clause he also explains: "a dead body may also be clothed, therefore he adds, Nor for your body, what you shall put on."

Chrysostom supplies the qualification without which the command is ruinous. "The words, Take no thought, are not the same as do no work, but, 'Have not your minds fixed on earthly things.'" And he adds the observation that makes the two compatible: "it so happens, that the man who is working takes no thought."

Cyril of Alexandria puts the argument as a proportion: the soul is more excellent than food and the body than clothing, so "God who has implanted that which is greater, how will He not give that which is less?" Ambrose reaches the same conclusion from physiology — nothing should convince believers more than that "the ethereal spirit perpetuates the vital union of the soul and body... without our exertion", so "it is absurd to suppose that a supply of food will be wanting to us, who are in possession of the everlasting substance of life".

Ambrose then says something none of the others will. Watching birds fed without tillage or harvest, he concludes that "the cause of our poverty seems to be covetousness" — the birds eat freely "because they think not of claiming to themselves by any special right fruits given for common food". The application is blunt: "we have lost what things were common by claiming them as our own", and in any case "neither is any thing a man's own, where nothing is perpetual, nor is supply certain when the end is uncertain".

Bede asks why the example is drawn from birds when Elijah, Moses and John were available as men who cared least for earthly things. His answer is precedent: Christ followed the Old Testament, "which sends us to the bee and the ant... in whom the Creator has implanted certain natural dispositions". On the comparison he is precise — men are more precious "because a rational animal like man is of a higher order in the nature of things than irrational things".

Why ravens rather than birds in general is Theophylact's question, and he offers three answers. First, natural history turned providential: ravens "produce indeed, but do not feed, but neglect their young, to whom in a marvelous manner from the air their food comes, brought as it were by the wind, which they receive having their mouths open" — the least parental of birds being the clearest case of God's feeding. Second, that the part stands for the whole, "spoken by synecdoche". Third, that where Matthew has the birds of the air Luke names ravens "as being more greedy and ravenous than others" — the greediest creature fed anyway.

Gill notices that what Matthew puts as a question Luke affirms, and that the Oriental versions strengthen it into a reason — seeing the life is more than meat. His inference is the plainest form of the argument here: life "is more excellent and valuable in its own nature, being that for the support of which meat is provided", and since God is its author "it need not be doubted but he will give meat for the maintenance and continuance of it".
25:
Wesley reads the cubit as idiom rather than measurement: to add a cubit to a thing "was a kind of proverbial expression for making the least addition to it". Gill takes the same view of what follows, glossing the least thing as adding to a man's stature "or rather to add one moment to his days". Robertson notes that the verse about the least thing is Luke's alone, absent from Matthew and dropped by one manuscript altogether; Ellicott, that it is "peculiar to St. Luke's report" and carries the argument further than Matthew does — if no anxiety can add a cubit or a day, "how much less can we control all the myriad contingencies upon which the happiness of the future may depend!"

Chrysostom takes the lilies apart phrase by phrase, and begins with the same caution he applied to the ravens. As the birds not sowing was no reproof of sowing "but all superfluous trouble", so the lilies not toiling "does not put an end to work, but to all anxiety about it". He then asks why lilies were chosen and not a showier creature: not "a swan or a peacock, but the lilies", because the argument needs force "on both sides, that is to say, both from the meanness of the things which have obtained such honor, and from the excellence of the honor conferred upon them".

The reading continues into the small words. A little later Christ "does not call them lilies, but grass"; he says not that tomorrow they are not, "but tomorrow is cast into the oven"; and "nor does He say simply, God clothe, but He says, God so clothe, which has much meaning" — while "how much more you" expresses "His estimation and care of the human race". Even the rebuke is weighed: when fault must be found he "deals here also with mildness, reproving them not for unbelief, but for littleness of faith", and the aim is not merely to stop anxiety about clothes but that we should "not even admire elegance in dress".

Eusebius answers the man who wants fine raiment by sending him to look harder at what he already despises. God "extends His manifold wisdom" even to the flowers of the field, "adorning them with divers colors, so adapting to the delicate membranes of the flowers dyes far superior to gold and purple" that no luxurious king, "not even Solomon himself", ever had such work devised for him. The comparison with Solomon is thus not rhetorical exaggeration but, on his account, a fair judgement about dyeing.

Ambrose thinks the comparison itself remarkable and worth pausing over — "nor does it seem of light moment, that a flower is either compared to man, or even almost more than to man is preferred to Solomon" — and reads the brightness upward, so that the colour is meant to convey the glory of the heavenly angels, "who are truly the flowers of the other world". Cyril of Alexandria draws the practical rule instead, that it suffices "to have a suitable garment, and moderate food, not exceeding what is enough", and that for the saints even that is superseded by "those spiritual delights which are in Christ".

Gill collects the versions and finds the flower unfixed: some copies read lilies of the field, the Persic has roses and lilies, the Arabic simply flowers — and he is content, since "what is afterwards said, is true of any of them". His note on the next verse dissolves the distinction entirely: lilies and tulips "are no other than grass, weak, frail, fading, short lived flowers, which have all their gaiety and beauty from the great Creator of them". Robertson keeps to the philology, noting a late form of the verb for clothing and the small difference that Matthew has grass of the field where Luke has grass in it.
29:
The verb behind "be not of doubtful mind" is rare, and the commentators disagree what it means. Robertson gives the history: from a word meaning high in midair — "our meteor" — it came to mean lifting oneself up with hopes, then being tossed like a ship, then anxiety and doubt, which he takes as the sense here. Clarke, citing Raphelius, makes it a mind "agitated with useless thoughts, and vain imaginations concerning food, raiment, and riches"; Barnes glosses it as living in careful suspense.

The fathers heard the same word differently. Augustine takes it as being puffed up rather than kept in suspense — "man first seeks these things to satisfy his wants, but when he is filled, he begins to be puffed up concerning them" — like a wounded man boasting "that he had many plasters in his house, whereas it were well for him that he had no wounds". Theophylact makes it instability: "an unsteady motion of the mind, meditating first one thing, then another, and jumping from this to that, and imagining lofty things."

Bede fixes what is forbidden, and the qualification cuts two ways. Christ "says not, Do not seek or take thought about meat, or drink, or raiment, but what you shall eat or drink", which reproves "those who, despising the common food and clothing, seek for themselves either more delicate or coarser food and clothing than theirs with whom they live" — conspicuous austerity falling under the same rebuke as luxury.

Gregory of Nyssa answers the objection that men have obtained "dominion and honors and riches by praying for them": God grants the lower petitions so that, learning he listens, "we may be raised to the desire of higher things" — as a child clings to the breast, "but when the child grows up it despises the milk".

Gill and Clarke note that "the nations of the world" is a fixed Jewish idiom for the Gentiles, and Clarke presses the verb: "to seek one thing after another, to be continually and eagerly coveting". His summary is a contrast: "it is the essence of heathenism to live only for this life; and it is the property of Christianity to lead men to live here in reference to another and better world." Robertson observes that Luke has neither first nor his righteousness nor all, where Matthew has all three.

Why the flock is little draws five explanations from Theophylact alone: those willing to be disciples; saints who "seem little because of their voluntary poverty"; those outnumbered by the angels; those fewer than the reprobate; "or rather because of their devout humility". Cyril of Alexandria turns the smallness into the argument: though the flock is little "both in nature and number and renown", the Father has granted it "the lot of heavenly spirits" — so "how shall He who gives such precious things be wearied in showing mercy towards you?"

How literally to sell is answered practically. Bede allows the selling and then requires the work: it is done worthily "when a man having once for his Lord's sake forsaken all that he has, nevertheless afterwards labors with his hands that he may be able both to gain his living, and give alms". Gill limits it to occasions, when providence calls and "rather than the poor should go without a supply". Barnes takes it as the condition of discipleship. Chrysostom commends the remedy: "there is no sin which almsgiving does not avail to blot out. It is a salve adapted to every wound."

Barnes reads the purse that never waxes old against the girdle-bag that does: "purses, here, grow old and useless. Wealth takes to itself wings." Clarke ends on the heart's habit of visiting its treasure "to see that all is safe and secure", producing a line of Plautus for it: "I am here; but my heart is at home, i.e. with my money."
35:
The command is a picture before it is a doctrine. Barnes, Ellicott and Wesley reconstruct the same scene: the long outer robe of the East had to be gathered into a sash before a man could work or run, so "to gird up the loins means to be ready, to be active, to be diligent". Robertson presses the grammar to the same end — both verbs are periphrastic imperatives, the lamps "already burning and continuously burning", not lit at the last moment. Gill spiritualises it into the girdle of truth, held "even unto death". Ellicott hears in the picture "the germ of the thought which was afterwards developed into the parable of the Wise and Foolish Virgins".

The fathers divide the two images and insist on their order. Theophylact takes girded loins for the active life and burning lamps for "the gift of discernment, that the active man may be able to distinguish not only what he ought to do, but in what way; otherwise men rush down the precipice of pride" — and notes that loins come first, "for first indeed comes action, then reflection, which is an enlightening of the mind". Gregory reads the girdle as continence and the lamp as visible work: "we hold burning lamps in our hands, when by good works we show forth bright examples to our neighbors." Augustine adds intention: the lamp must burn "with a true end and right intention". Cyril of Alexandria makes girding a readiness "to undergo evils from regard to Divine love".

Whose wedding it is gets three answers. Gregory says he went to it in ascending, when "as the Bridegroom He joined to Himself the heavenly multitude of angels"; Theophylact says he is daily betrothing the souls of saints, and returns "perhaps to all at the end of the whole world... perhaps also every hour standing suddenly present at the death of each individual". Cyril of Alexandria will not let the festival end: he comes from the wedding as from a feast "which God is ever keeping; for nothing can cause sadness to the Incorruptible Nature".

Gregory's reading of the knock is the sharpest here. "He comes when He hastens to judgment, but He knocks, when already by the pain of sickness He denotes that death is at hand" — and the state of the soul is exposed by which way it moves: "he who trembles to depart from the body, has no wish to open to the Judge knocking, and dreads to see that Judge whom he remembers to have despised", while he who is secure "grows joyful, because of the glory of his reward".

The reversal — the master girding himself to serve — is felt by all. Lightfoot puts it plainly: "the master will pass by his dignity, and condescend to minister to his own servants." Ellicott sends it to the upper room, where the act "must have reminded the disciples of the words which are recorded here", and to Revelation 3:20, adding that the promise balances "the seeming harshness of the Master in Luke 17:8". Robertson blocks the sentimental version: Jesus washed feet "not out of gratitude, but to give the apostles an object lesson in humility".

Then the figure changes. Robertson quotes Bruce: "the Master returning from a wedding is replaced by a thief whose study it is to come to the house he means to plunder at an unexpected time." Theophylact reports and rejects the reading that makes the thief the devil and the house the soul, "for the Lord's coming is compared to the thief as suddenly at hand". Lightfoot dates the watches: the second and third are "the very dead time of sleep". Cyril of Jerusalem draws the practical edge — "as to the time let no one be curious... venture not thou to declare when these things shall be, nor on the other hand supinely slumber."
41:
Peter's interruption is treated as historical rather than literary. Robertson notes that everything from verse 22 has been addressed to the disciples, so the question is unsurprising, and that it "confirms also the impression that Luke is giving actual historical data in the environment of these discourses" — impulsive like the interruption on the mount of transfiguration, and "certainly more than a literary device of Luke". Henry has Peter "now, as often, spokesman for the disciples", and draws an unexpected caution: "we have reason to bless God that there are some such forward men, that have a gift of utterance; let those that are such take heed of being proud."

What Peter was actually asking is disputed. Bede rules out the obvious reading: "it is marvelous if Peter doubted that all must live soberly, piously, and justly, who wait for a blessed hope, or that the judgment will to each and all be unexpected." The question must concern what he might not know — "whether those sublime commands of a heavenly life in which He bade us sell what we have and provide bags which wax not old, and watch with our loins girded, belonged to the Apostles only, and those like to them, or to all who were to be saved." He offers three possible senses of us and all: apostles against ordinary believers; Christians against unbelievers; or those who die singly against those found alive at the universal judgment. Ellicott, reading Peter through Matthew 19:27, thinks not the warning but the promise of verse 37 provoked him — was that "the common blessing of all believers, or the special reward of those who had forsaken all?"

The answer is oblique. Gill observes that Christ "does not directly, and in express words, answer to Peter's question", and Wesley agrees that the reply "manifestly implies, that he had spoken this parable primarily (though not wholly) to the ministers of his word". Henry cuts the knot with Mark 13:37 — "what I say unto you, I say unto all" — while still holding the sequel adapted to ministers. Robertson notes the form: a rhetorical question "that answers itself. Peter is this wise steward, each of the Twelve is, anyone is who acts thus."

Theophylact explains why both qualities are named, symmetrically: "whether a man be careless yet faithful to his master, or else wise yet unfaithful, the things of the master perish." His illustration is unusually candid — "I have known many servants of God, and faithful men, who because they were unable to manage ecclesiastical affairs, have destroyed not only possessions, but souls, exercising towards sinners indiscreet virtue by extravagant rules of penance or unseasonable indulgence." Faithfulness without competence is not safe.

Augustine notes that Christ "says portion, because of suiting His measure to the capacity of his several hearers"; Theophylact takes it as "either the word of doctrine by which their souls are fed, or the example of works by which their life is fashioned"; Henry gives the rule as suum cuique, "to every one his own. This is rightly to divide the word of truth." Clarke adds that Jewish stewards provided "not only food, but raiment". Robertson's word study confirms the register: the rare compound rendered portion of meat is found nowhere else in Greek until Deissmann turned it up "in an Egyptian papyrus and then an inscription in Lycia".

On the promotion Augustine goes furthest: he is set "not only over His own household, but that earthly things as well as heavenly shall obey him. As it was with Joshua the son of Nun, and Elias, the one commanding the sun, the other the clouds." Henry stays nearer the ground, comparing Joseph's rise in Pharaoh's court. Wesley alone leaves the door open the other way: "God himself pronounces him wise, faithful, happy! Yet we see, he might fall from all, and perish for ever."
45:
Gill keeps the two servants apart: this is not the wise steward gone bad, but "another... in a like post, and in the same office, but is an evil servant, as Matthew calls him". The vocabulary is domestic. Ellicott notes that menservants is literally "the boys", used "like the French garçon... for servants of any age", and that Luke's terms are more specific than Matthew's "fellow-servants"; Robertson adds that the feminine is a diminutive, "originally just a damsel", found in the papyri.

Robertson notes the verb for cutting asunder is rare, only here and in Matthew, and "used literally here". The phrase that follows is corrected by three commentators at once. Robertson denies the usual sense: not "the unbelieving" but "the unreliable, the untrustworthy"; Ellicott prefers "the unfaithful", the word "affording sharp contrast with the faithful and wise steward"; Clarke presses the difference against the heathen, who "knew not the will of God... and, though they acted against it, did not do it in obstinacy; the former knew that will, and daringly opposed it." Wesley draws the line the others leave implicit: it is "his everlasting portion, with the unfaithful — as faithful as he was once, God himself being the Judge!"

Robertson notes that the agreement with Matthew 24:51 ends here and Luke alone preserves what follows, leaving the standing alternative: "we must either think that Jesus repeated the parable or that one of the writers has misplaced it." Ellicott calls the remaining verses "peculiar to St. Luke, and every word is full of profoundest interest", hearing in the warning to those "sinning against light and knowledge" a latent reference to Judas.

The stripes are a legal measure, not a figure. Lightfoot supplies the puzzle: forty was the ceiling, yet a man could be sentenced to fourscore — "they might not exceed that number for one single crime: but if the crime was doubled, they might double the punishment" — and wonders whether Paul's accusers multiplied charges to multiply his. Clarke repeats the solution, crediting Lightfoot; Barnes adds that lesser offences drew four, five or six.

The fathers turn the gradation on the clergy. Theophylact makes the dignity the aggravation: "the greatness of his dignity shall the rather become a cause of his condemnation". Chrysostom states the principle: "greater knowledge is an occasion of greater punishment. Therefore shall the Priest, committing the same sin with the people, suffer a far heavier penalty." Cyril of Alexandria explains why the plea fails: the man of understanding sins "inexcusably, departing as it were maliciously from the will of God", while "the rude or unlearned man will more reasonably ask for pardon". Theophylact faces the objection that ignorance should not be punished, and answers that it is culpable: "when he might have known, he would not, but being himself slothful, was the cause of his own ignorance." Calvin agrees — "our ignorance is always accompanied by gross and shameful negligence" — and reads verse 48 agriculturally: the favoured man who fails to yield more, "like a field which has been cultivated at greater expense", finds the abuse of grace costs him dear.

Whether the graded stripes limit the sentence is contested. Basil is blunt: the passage "assigns neither measure nor end of punishments, but their differences. For a man may deserve unquenchable fire, to a slight or more intense degree of heat." Ellicott lets the same words "throw a gleam of hope on the darkness that lies behind the veil", and declines to decide "whether the few stripes imply limited duration, or suffering less acute, an older tolerabilior damnatio". Bede sits between: mildest of all is theirs "who, beyond the guilt they originally contracted, have added none besides". Theophylact and Ellicott agree on the last distinction: what is given and what is committed differ, the latter a deposit to be increased, "for the grace of the word needs increase".
49:
Robertson catches the tone before the sense: "suddenly Jesus lets the volcano in his own heart burst forth". Ellicott hears the same break — "a strange unique abruptness in the utterance... a pause, a moment's thought, as in one whose gaze looks out into the future, and who at once feels its terrors and yet accepts them."

What the fire is gets five answers that do not reduce to one. Gill offers the gospel itself, which "gives both light and heat... though very distressing and torturing to wicked men", or zeal for it, or "the fiery trial; which tries men, as gold is tried in the fire". Barnes makes it "the emblem of discord and contention". Ellicott makes it judgment, "which shall purify and cleanse as well as destroy". Clarke doubles it: the Roman sword and "the influence of his own Spirit in the destruction of sin", already kindled but "as yet... but a spark". Wesley alone hears no threat — "to spread the fire of heavenly love over all the earth". Calvin refuses to choose: one fire, two effects, for "the same fire of doctrine, when it burns on all sides, consumes chaff and straw, but purifies silver and gold."

The half-sentence that follows is admitted to be obscure. Robertson says outright that "it is not clear what this passage means", then reads the interrogative as how: "How I wish that it were already kindled." Barnes paraphrases the same way, "And what would I, but that it were kindled". Lightfoot solves it as an idiom of the schools, where What do I say? means I do say this: "What will I? is the same with This I will", so the sense is "This I will, that it be already kindled."

The metaphor then changes element. Robertson quotes Plummer's antithesis: "the world is lit up with flames and Christ is bathed in blood." Gill takes the baptism as the sufferings and makes the word argue for immersion — Christ "was as it were immersed, or plunged into them", a sense "almost all interpreters observe on the text, and by which they confess the true import and primary signification of the word". Ellicott locates the pain precisely: what he felt most keenly "was the pain, the constraint of expectation... harassed and oppressed, as other sufferers have been, by the thought of what was coming, more than by the actual suffering when it came." Robertson notes that the verb for that constraint is the one Paul uses of his longing to depart. Wesley is plainest: "I must suffer first, before I can set up my kingdom." Calvin fixes the order: the first-fruits are offered in Christ's own person, "after which the disciples ought not to be displeased at feeling some portion of it."

Calvin states the sharpest objection against himself: the prophets promise peace under Christ's reign, and Christ is called our peace, so kindled war "does not seem to agree with the predictions of the prophets, and still less with the office of Christ". His answer is that this peace "has no existence but among the sincere worshippers of God"; to unbelievers "the message of peace excites in them a greater tumult than before", so that Christ, "the author of [peace], becomes the occasion of disturbances in consequence of the wickedness of men." Robertson is blunter: "peace at any price is not the purpose of Christ... loyalty to Christ counts more than all else."

Gill resolves the arithmetic of the five: the mother and the mother-in-law "are one and the same person, only standing in different relations". Cyril of Jerusalem reports an unexpected use: Archelaus turned the verse on Mani, who had called the God of the Old Testament evil for saying I am a consuming fire — "whose Son is He who saith, I came to send fire on the earth?"
54:
The audience changes. Gill notes that what preceded went to the disciples, and that Christ now turns to the multitude, "and particularly addressed himself to the Scribes and Pharisees that were among them"; Henry makes it a rule of ministry — "he preached ad populum, to the people, as well as ad clerum, to the clergy." Theophylact supplies the connection backwards: after hearing preaching called a sword, the hearers "may have been troubled, not knowing what He meant", so the weather signs are offered as something they can read.

The meteorology is local. Wesley, Gill and Barnes agree: the west wind blows off the sea and brings rain, the south comes over Arabia, Egypt and Ethiopia and brings sultry heat. Henry hears the Hebrew idiom behind the west, "out of the sea", and remembers the cloud "no bigger than a man's hand" of 1 Kings 18:44. Ellicott sharpens the second sign: the word for heat probably means "the burning wind, the simoom, which, blowing over the desert, scorched and withered all that was green and fresh." Robertson notes similar sayings stand in Matthew with enough difference of phrasing that whether it is "difference of source or different use of the same source... we do not know."

Henry presses the epistemology in praise of experience: the prognostications "had their origin in repeated observations upon the chain of causes: from what has been we conjecture what will be", and art has since "improved the notices of nature in weather-glasses" — yet "nature has not tied itself to such a track but that sometimes we are mistaken." Basil defends the practice on the same ground: "conjectures concerning the stars are necessary to the life of man, as long as we do not push our searches into their signs beyond due limits" — the sailor must foresee storms, the husbandman his harvest.

Theophylact reads Christ into both images. "I am a cloud, and I come out of the west, that is, from human nature; which has been long since clothed with the thick darkness of sin... For I am the strong south wind, opposed to the northern coldness." Cyril of Alexandria keeps the eschatology without the identification: the shower is "a future punishment by fire", the heat "the time of salvation, that is, the coming of the Savior" — and "ignorance of the time to come" will not "avail them after the present life."

Bede closes the escape route twice. Those who can predetermine the weather "might if they wished also understand the time of our Lord's coming from the words of the Prophets"; and lest anyone plead ignorance of the prophetic books, the next verse shows that "although unlearned they might still by their natural ability discern Him, who did works such as none other man did, to be above man, and to be God." Origen states the premise it needs: "had it not been implanted in our nature to judge what is right, our Lord would never have said this."

What the hypocrisy consists of is put three ways. Robertson makes it perceptual, calling them to "test as spiritual chemists", their blindness "when looking at and hearing him" persisting in "those who are willfully blind to the steps of God among men". Clarke and Barnes make it inferential: miracles and prophets stand to the Messiah's arrival as cloud to shower — "why do you not, in like manner, infer that this is the time when the Messiah should appear?" Henry makes it a failure of will rather than sight: they "pretend to expect the Messiah and his kingdom, and yet are no way disposed to receive and entertain it" — "now is the accepted time, now or never." Ellicott names what was missed: it was "the time of their visitation... and yet they knew it not."
57:
Ellicott narrows the opening question: "the meaning of the words is not that they did not know what was right, but that they did not act upon their knowledge." They were judging, and judging badly — "passing an unrighteous judgment on the preachers of repentance, on the Baptist and on the Christ." He raises and declines a link back to verse 13: possibly, "though not, I think, probable", the question glances at the request that Christ act as judge. Calvin diagnoses rather than describes: Christ "opens up the source of the evil, and, as it were, applies the lancet to the ulcer", the failure being a refusal to sit still — hypocrites "throw their swelling words into the air without any concern, and never exercise calm thought, or place themselves at the tribunal of God." Robertson turns it into an argument: even "without the presence and teaching of Jesus they had light enough to tell what is right and so without excuse as Paul argued" in the opening chapters of Romans.

Ellicott corrects the opening — "better, with all the MSS., For as thou goest", the conjunction dropped by translators "because they did not see the sequence of thought implied in it". Chrysostom holds the scene down to earth: "it seems to me that He is speaking of the present judges, and of the way to the present judgment, and of the prison of this world" — a lesson from things "visible and at hand", pitched "for the sake of His ruder hearers." Gill agrees the man is "a bad man, that will not pay his just debts"; Theophylact draws the counsel: "although you have nothing, borrow in order that you may be released from him."

The allegorists take every figure. Ambrose names three adversaries — the devil, "every vicious practice", and "an evil conscience, which affects us both in this world, and will accuse and betray us in the next" — then makes the magistrate the Father, the judge Christ, and the officers the angels who "sever the wicked from among the just". Bede makes the adversary the word of God, "which opposes our carnal desires in this life; from which he is delivered who is subject to its precepts". Origen's scheme is most elaborate: two angels attend every man, and the bad one "whenever we sin rejoices, knowing that he has an occasion for exaltations and boasting with the prince of the world, who sent him". Escape is by "having wisdom, justice, fortitude, and temperance"; the officer "has no power to let me off even a farthing", being "one appointed by the master to demand the debts". Ellicott holds both readings together: the adversary is "the Law that accuses them", the judge "none other than the Judge of all the earth".

The lexical detail favours the literal frame. Clarke renders the imperative "give labor, do every thing in thy power to get free before a suit commences", and identifies the officer, on Kypke's authority, as one "appointed to levy the fines imposed by the law"; Robertson agrees, reads the verb for being quit of him as a perfect, "to be rid of him for good", and derives the coin from a verb meaning "to peel off the bark".

Whether the debt is ever paid divides them. Origen allows gradations, since "he who has been guilty of a great debt, will have endless ages for his payment"; Ambrose lets satisfaction cancel it, as interest is discharged when the principal is. Bede shuts the door: the prisoner "will ever have to pay the penalty by suffering, but never by paying it obtain pardon". Clarke turns the same fact against the spiritual reading altogether: "can weeping, wailing, and gnashing of teeth, pay to Divine justice the debt a sinner has contracted? This is impossible: let him who readeth understand." Wesley presses urgency: "ye have not a moment to lose."
